newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - South African taxis prey to Mafia-style hitmen.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - South African taxis prey to Mafia-style hitmen.

text.p: South Africa's fiercely competitive minibus taxi industry, once hailed as a beacon of black economic advancement, has fallen prey to Mafia-style hitmen -- and passengers are often the victims.
In the last two years alone, more than 540 passengers and drivers have died in the fight for profitable routes as attackers spray rival vehicles with automatic gunfire at taxi ranks in the rush hour.
"Crime syndicates are using well-paid hitmen. They are very clever -- they work in a certain way to eliminate people in the industry," police chief George Fivaz told reporters.
"The lid that police successes have put on the boiling pot of taxi violence is now in danger of being lifted by intensified tensions and naked aggression within the industry," Fivaz said.
He said even his own officers seem to be involved. Four policemen are among the 57 people arrested so far this year on suspicion of belonging to taxi hit squads.

Frank van der Velde, a former Cape Town councillor and onetime mediator between the taxi organisations, believes President Nelson Mandela's government should impose strict regulations on the industry.

"Fundamentally, the industry is overtraded and this fact leaves a basic problem for the taxi owner who, because of the stiff competition for fewer passengers, cannot meet his obligations," van der Velde told Reuters.
"Whether the government likes it or not, it is going to have to regulate this industry," he said. "The lack of regulation has led to a chaotic situation and commuters are suffering."

In Cape Town recently, a passing motorist was killed in a shootout on the city's major highway, the N2 which leads to Cape Town international airport and is regularly used by tourists. Six people were injured.
The taxi business became popular among black entrepreneurs during the apartheid era as one of a few business avenues open to them.
Some 90,000 taxi operators, half of whom work illegally, are being offered a one-off chance for a licence by the transport ministry, which hopes this will help regulate pirate operators.

Transport Minister Mac Maharaj has acknowledged that conflicts will not be resolved merely by mediation and law enforcement: "That is not feasible given what we inherited and the anarchy in this industry."

Fivaz called on the government to introduce rules to address the problems of market saturation, large taxi monopolies trying to squeeze out smaller operators, and the shortage of adequate infrastructure.
Despite the bloody conflict, more than half of all black commuters have no other way home. Trains are overcrowded and the network limited. Buses are few and far between.
Apart from the danger of being caught in crossfire, passengers are among road users most likely to be involved in an accident.
Last year 1,083 people were killed in more than 67,000 accidents involving taxis.
One reason is that cash-strapped taxi owners skimp on new tyres and other safety features, but here again some people see the long arm of apartheid.
"Road users' aggressive attitudes have two main sources," said Eric Wise, director of transport management in Gauteng province.
"On one hand we have a group of (black) people who have not been entitled to use the roads, who have now found a freedom they didn't have before and are spreading their wings.

"On the other hand, we have a group of people for whom the army was part and parcel of turning 18," Wise said, referring to the former compulsory military service for white youth, who may now seek other outlets for their aggression.
